title: Universities’ social licence is founded on their impact – but funding matters too
summary: Debbie McVitty was at the annual gathering of university vice chancellors and finds a sector eager to prove its value – but are ministers on the same page?
full_text:
The annual Universities UK conference serves many purposes but one of these is a public dialogue about the state of the nation when it comes to higher education.

And this year’s conference confirms that “social licence” – a term whose origins lie outside HE but that has developed currency in HE outside the UK in the last decade, as Michael Salmon explains here – has now achieved full official cut-through in the UK as a guiding principle for situating universities in wider society.

The core argument runs as follows: despite the many well-evidenced ways that universities serve useful and valued social ends, public appreciation of their value cannot be taken for granted – and nor can the belief that what has produced that value in the past will automatically do so in the future.

Universities UK’s Future Universities project is explicitly intended to secure universities’ social licence for the future, positioning universities as critical to the country’s long term success. Each strand of the project – jobs, communities, students, innovation – tests the degree to which universities’ thinking and practice needs to evolve to meet contemporary public expectations of the sector. And the project as a whole aims to signal to government the sector’s preparedness to change and adapt, to be what the country needs it to be – and emphasise that it can be trusted to adapt from within rather than change being imposed from without.

As Universities UK president Malcolm Press expressed it in his conference speech:

Universities operate with what might be called a social licence: the trust and consent of the public to exercise considerable autonomy, educate future generations and receive amounts of substantial tax payer money. This licence cannot be taken for granted. It is sustained only through the value of what we provide, the outcomes we achieve, and the way that we behave.

Taking the notion of social licence at face value, there are two key corollaries. One is that institutions that put that collective social licence at risk should expect to meet cold shoulders from the rest of the sector. Here’s how Press put it:

A values-based membership organisation must support its members, but it must also be prepared to challenge them. Solidarity cannot mean silence when practices damage students, communities or confidence in universities as a whole.

It’s not quite “keep your nose clean or we’ll kick you out of our club” but it’s a shot across the bows of any institution that’s courting risk, most likely to be around international recruitment and external partnerships, that could blow up if not carefully handled.

The second is that the case for political attention and sustainable funding rests on a public value and impact argument – higher education only commands political support to the extent it delivers value, not on its own terms. But if the government does not deliver that political support and sustainable funding settlement, that public value and impact is put at risk.

That’s why the sector is pressing the government to lock in indexation of fees (which has been promised but for which there is no schedule for delivery) and to look again at the planned international levy. It is why Universities UK has announced its plans to develop a broader range of measures that can capture the value that universities deliver (first mooted in the 2024 Blueprint for change). It’s also why Press called for a “long term partnership framework” with government – by implication, if the sector does its bit, government ought to step up and play its part.

Warmish words

To listen to skills minister Jacqui Smith and newly appointed science minister Chris McDonald talk, you’d think the government bought fully into the premise. The Prime Minister, Smith reported, wants to “empower” universities to be part of place-based growth. The target of two-thirds participation in higher education (of all kinds) remains in place in the post-Starmer era. International students are welcome in the UK. The government has put higher education on a firmer financial footing (to be enacted “when parliamentary time allows”) and set out in its post-16 white paper a direction of travel for the sector (just in case we were in any doubt about whether that white paper still applies in the new world order).

Smith also announced that to help universities and colleges make informed decisions around regional higher education and skills provision the government plans to develop a market monitoring tool to capture data on gaps in education supply and demand, available provision, and research strengths. McDonald showed the sector his formidable credentials as an engineer and industry partner to universities, reassured on his commitment to discovery-led research, and spoke about the Prime Minister’s agenda to “put science in the service of industry” – especially through ensuring discoveries made in the UK realise benefit in the UK economy rather than elsewhere.

None of this is hostile, and much of it is useful, but it’s not the honest confrontation with political and economic realities that could form the basis of a partnership framework. We don’t expect deep analysis or policy detail from ministers in set-piece speeches, but you might reasonably expect a minister familiar with the challenges universities are wrestling with to show some appreciation of the contours of the problem.

The skills minister might, without any loss of government credibility, have acknowledged that devolution arrangements are patchy and require time to mature, that the market for modular provision needs help to grow, that expansion of technical and apprenticeship forms of higher education are bounded by employer capacity, and that priorities will need to be set in places on the basis of resource scarcity.

The closest the sector got to a real offer of dialogue around a shared challenge was McDonald arguing that the research grant application system is a “value-destroying activity” for research and researchers and soliciting views on how to reduce bureaucracy in the interests of getting research funded more quickly. Nothing to sneeze at, unless you love research bureaucracy, but not really touching the sides of the larger shifts in research funding that institution heads are anticipating.

A vacancy on the other side of the table

Complaining about politicians doing politics is obviously a bit of a mug’s game, but it speaks directly to the limits of “social licence” as an organising principle for the sector’s thinking about its future. Social licence is ambiguous depending on the scale of the imagined community whose licence you are trying to secure. What is driving the national conversation about value is rather different to the local context – nationally it’s about net migration, graduate returns and to some extent issues around free speech and student protest. These issues are university-specific manifestations of a larger crisis of confidence in politics, the economy and the security of future generations, rather than anything any single university can control, though the sector is right to offer its services in helping to address them.

Meanwhile, locally, social licence is a function of relationships of trust. Erosion of that licence, as one conference speaker put it, could be indicated by a lower willingness to invest in shared work, or loss of local support and championing. However, many universities would point out that local partners are more eager than ever to work with their university, because of wider financial pressures across the public and third sectors. The pinch comes when universities have to make choices about where they can invest in partnerships and – as one vice chancellor observed – make painful job cuts that affect local employment and resonate negatively in communities. Ultimately it does come down to funding and financial sustainability.

And this is where it all starts to unwind. Universities are seeking to reconfigure themselves and adapt to a different resource landscape. They are exploring how to lock into their places in more innovative and strategic ways, and trying to manage expectations. They can do more to measure what matters and do what counts most. They can begin to stress-test long standing assumptions about what higher education needs to be and how it should work – I’ve noticed with some amusement that higher education appears to be entering its “provocation” era and actively soliciting the expression of ideas that can challenge the status quo (a good example being Post-18 Project director John Blake’s presentation to vice chancellors last week).

In all of this work a partnership framework with government would be tactically and strategically useful to the sector, securing government backing and, arguably, political cover, for necessary change. Channelling reform of the sector through policy and political leadership would give it a greater sense of democratic legitimacy rather than individual institutions making piecemeal decisions, albeit in good faith. But partnership takes bandwidth, continuous engagement, and the willingness to put credibility and resource commitments on the table to deliver a common purpose. And despite the warm words, this government still doesn’t look like it’s ready to take that step with the higher education sector.

title: Higher education finances are “under review” – but what does that mean?
summary: It is the Treasury that gets to decide on any changes to sector funding, and it is the state of public finances that determines that there will be no major rethink. David Kernohan has been listening to the chancellor
full_text:
As a rule, we don’t get major funding policy announcements when ministers responsible for higher education address the Universities UK conference.

In recent years it has been a moment for making a room full of increasingly anxious vice chancellors feel loved – perhaps garnished with an ask connecting the work of the sector to other government priorities.

This time round, Jacqui Smith – in a comparatively rare in-person appearance – said she was keen to continue working on “financial stability.” Later in the speech, she highlighted the inflationary fee cap increase as a means of offering some much-requested “long term financial certainty,” though she stopped short of explaining when this long term commitment would reach the statute book.

For a room dealing with those “difficult choices” driven by years of “financial pressure” there is a limit to the good that financial certainty will do. It feels redundant to note that an inflationary increase to home undergraduate fees provides – at best – a real-terms maintenance of the value of home fees. Provided recruitment holds up – in the face of a tightening graduate jobs market and costs rising above inflationary maintenance increases for students.

The government line, thus far, has been that the higher education funding system in England is “under review”. We saw it again in the governments’ response to a damning Treasury Committee inquiry report: an “ongoing consideration of higher education funding and student support arrangements.”

Work in progress

As best we can tell, this review is a desk exercise underway within the Department for Education. Civil servants are paying attention to the wider socio-economic benefits of higher education, beyond the improved earnings return to individual graduates. And on that, we’ve seen a more thorough (if still imperfect) analysis as to whether these returns compare to what a similarly-qualified person secured via a non-degree route.

What doesn’t seem to be happening parallel to this is a detailed analysis of costs (rather than prices) within the higher education sector. There’s not really a dataset beyond TRAC that can easily be brought to bear – there’s nothing since the Augar review annexes (2019!) that engages critically with the cost of educating undergraduate students as opposed to the price. To be clear, ministers and officials do meet regularly with senior leaders and sector representative groups – they will not be unaware of what is going on in the sector.

The other notable trend has been an analysis of the costs to graduates presented by (largely the plan 2) student loan repayment system. This campaign started outside the government – in the journalism of the millennial cohort currently affected – and focuses largely on the interest rate applied to loans. The government response has been to apply the fee cap at 6 per cent – not far off the inflation plus three per cent maximum that would otherwise work out at about 6.2 per cent, but a sensible hedge against likely future rises (there are already hints that the Bank of England are thinking about multiple rises) in the rate of inflation.

To be clear, the plan 2 interest rates are causing young graduates real problems. This weeks’ edition of The Rest is Politics saw Labour PPS Rosie Wrighting talk about the £80,000 she currently owes, the way she feels “lied to” about the rewards for her hard work, and you’d be hard pressed not to agree with her. She studied fashion – a major export industry for the UK, and one of those facets of industry that has a positive impact on the lives of many. Short sighted pronouncements about the “worth” of degrees make us all poorer – while also doing nothing to address youth poverty.

DfE is looking largely at tweaks to the current system, not whole-scale reform. As Jacqui Smith told the House of Lords “Income-contingent student loans and grants are an equitable way of funding higher education, as individuals who benefit financially from higher-level study make a fair contribution towards its cost, while lower earners are protected.” The clearest signal we have on any change relates to the Strategic Priority Grant – the Education and Skills White Paper hints at a “a targeted approach to funding provision that drives growth in priority sectors.”

Treasury brain

All of this represents important and valuable work, but it will not – by itself – change the way higher education is funded in England. The work that DfE is engaged in will inform a submission (a very telling word) to the Treasury. It is John Healey, Lucy Rigby, and Emma Reynolds – not Lucy Powell and Jacqui Smith – that will make the final determinations as to the future funding of the sector.

Ahead of his first budget, scheduled for 28 October, Healey has been setting out his priorities via a substantial interview with the Financial Times, and a speech delivered at the Midlands Technology Centre on 7 September. Our new chancellor is popularly painted as the man that says “no” – a brake to Andy Burnham’s instinct to spend to solve problems. That’s a common enough dynamic between Chancellor and Prime Minister; after all, the latter has a responsibility to run a popular government, while the former aspires to fund a responsible and sustainable administration.

Healey’s most notable characteristic is a willingness to think long term. He reminded the FT that: “some of the decisions I must take – and will take – will show the benefits in years to come” noting that he would not necessarily be in post to take the credit for these decisions. The most startling element of the MTC speech was a cut to the Green Book discount rate, which has the immediate impact of making measures that pay off in the medium term look more financially attractive.

I wrote about discount rates on Wonkhe recently if you want to get into the technicalities, but suffice it to say that under current rules predictions of future returns are scaled (by 3.5 per cent for each year ahead) to take account of what economists call a “time preference”: people generally prefer benefit now rather than the promise of a future benefit. Healey cut this rate from 3.5 per cent to 3 per cent to “skew investment towards projects with more long-term potential.”

This came alongside the introduction of an economic potential analysis, which brings place (that signature Burnham theme) into the equation. The line here is that this will allow government investment in local areas to be assessed “not on what they are today, but on what they could become in the future.”

Future benefits to current spending

In both these cases the Chancellor appears to be talking about capital investment – as you would expect, longer term benefits are often derived from one-off spending (building projects, start up costs) rather than maintenance of existing infrastructure via recurrent funding. But the gap between the two is smaller than you might imagine – an unmaintained system loses future value over time, and eventually collapses.

The challenge for DfE and the sector here is one of repositioning. The earnings (and spillover) returns from higher education are very much a future benefit for the nation. Very few graduates see the value of their degree reflected in what they do a year or so after graduation (despite this being where most of our data about graduate destinations is focused – even the ten years after graduation we see as the limits of LEO earnings data mean comparatively little in a system where loan repayments extend for 40 years and people expect to be earning well into their sixties.

We don’t use the discount rate to think about the funding system for higher education – most of the economic scaffold around loan repayments is focused on the allocation of the “subsidy” that means lower paid graduates get an effective fee discount. This works almost like a discount rate – benefits in later years are significantly reduced, but it has a regressive impact as the design of the system ensures that the lowest paid graduates contribute more than their better paid cohort over a lifetime of earning.

The movement to watch here comes from Bridget Phillipson’s announcement that section 1 of the 2010 Equality Act will (finally!) be commenced supported by the work of a new “Class Unit.” A duty on public bodies to ensure that users of state systems are not disadvantaged by their socio-economic status makes the regressive nature of the current loan system open to judicial review – a classic, discount-rate style, treatment of all repayments feels more defensible in a plan 5 system without real interest. And this would also serve to make the substantial contribution the government makes to the system (ministers claim around 30 to 40 per cent, though I put it a fair bit lower than that) visible.

Growth

Like most of his predecessors, Healey is keen to be seen as making financially responsible decisions, but also making investment in order to drive growth. And happily for the sector, he’s clear that innovation and skills are key mechanisms to drive growth.

The terms of the innovation pitch are interesting – it is linked in the mind of the chancellor both to research and development (“our science and research base is world-beating”) and to regulatory reform. A substantial portion of his speech in Birmingham was devoted to reducing the burden of regulation: cutting regulation by 25 per cent by the end of parliament, and making practical changes where business is being held back.

Since 2017, English higher education has been a regulated system – though the avowed “risk based” approach of the Office for Students has not been something that has had a great deal of impact on the administrative overheads of higher education providers.

I want to be clear here that I’m not talking about reductions in the size of the cadre of professional administrators that are needed to run a modern university – the regulatory burden comes about through onerous and often duplicated requirements for documentation and data that take substantial time (and contribute to the very real and growing problem of specialist staff burn-out).

The Chancellor directed a surprising amount of ire at “consultation culture”, but it was clear that he wasn’t against the transparency and willingness to allow other voices into the policy development process that consultation at its very best engenders. We’ve all experienced the other end of the consultation quality curve, hefty regulatory documentation that almost never changes as a result of your responses. Consultation response rates across government have (outside of high profile campaigns) been falling, and it is this common sense that your thinking is disappearing into a black hole – and it has to be said that the Office for Students do not cover themselves in glory here.

Recent years have seen any number of parliamentary, departmental, and legal excoriations handed out to the OfS. The new leadership has made the right noises about improving in response to these challenges, but it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to prevent a more radical curtailing of responsibilities. OfS is the only policy-making body outside of DfE in the whole post-16 education space – a recognition that higher education is unique and important among a wider post-compulsory offer. A strong regulator should be reinforcing, not undermining this special status.

Borrowing

Government borrowing has been at a historic high ever since the Covid emergency. Interest payments on this borrowing have, as we were reminded in the MPC speech, risen to a level more than equivalent to annual Department for Education spending. And the cost of new borrowing – while still substantially cheaper than that available to anyone or anything else – has risen sharply for the government: 10 year gilt rates are nudging 5 per cent on a regular basis, having never really recovered from Kwasi Kwarteng’s mini-budget.

Healey is alive to this issue. Reducing the cost of existing borrowing will be expensive and will entail a number of those “difficult choices” that parliamentarians like to talk about. Any new spending will require new borrowing, and the appetite for that at the Treasury is about as low as you could imagine. Higher education has already got an inflationary loan increase – and what is likely to end up being a costly expansion of the loan model to modular courses. Few other sectors have been this lucky.

The sector, and the commentary that surrounds it, is frustrated by the lack of consideration given to more radical changes to higher education funding – it is this lack of financial flexibility that drives the focus on fixing or modifying what we have. It’s the reason for the International Student Fee Levy: this unwelcome intervention provides a pot of money drawn largely from the more established and more financially stable end of the sector that can (hopefully – we await the details) be spent on other parts of higher education, including the promised limited return of the student grant.

Any radical proposal for reform has to take account of the debt already in the system that will take decades to resolve at an uncertain rate of return. It ideally has to address generational unfairness where graduate contributions are lower – and this is where the growing interest in longer term returns to government spending also comes into play.

Technically bleak

There is, therefore, no magic wand that will fix higher education funding to the satisfaction of students, providers, and the tax payer. The solutions that do emerge will be marginal gains at best, founded on an understanding of the wider value that higher-level skills, innovation, and the growing understanding around secondary and tertiary benefits brings.

The work that is ongoing may feel like tinkering while a system is in crisis. That’s because the environment in which these decisions are made has never been less welcoming. Government spending will rise, inevitably, as the focus turns to longer term problems and longer term benefits, and we should welcome Treasury recognition of this. Addressing the problems caused by climate change, and the prospect of an aging population with lower retirement savings, are the civilisation level challenges that will be front and centre in budget preparations – paying for work like that will be the second item of business. Everything else is lucky to be on the agenda at all.

Higher education has a civilisational benefit – and we should welcome DfE work to develop a better articulation of this, because vibes and storytelling are clearly not working. I’ve always been interested in the long-term, and would tentatively suggest that a civilisation that preserves itself without art, learning, and a sense of community is probably a civilisation in name only. But as always, such sentiments need to find their way onto a spreadsheet.

title: Universities Produce Talent. Economies Produce Returns.

The post Universities Produce Talent. Economies Produce Returns. appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join the Policy Institute at King’s College London and HEPI on Tuesday 15 September, from 6.30pm to 7.45pm, at Bush House, London, for a free event exploring the future of higher education in England. Drawing on Professor Sir Chris Husbands’ report, New choices: Revisiting futures for higher education in England, the discussion will consider how financial pressures, generative AI, changing student expectations and declining public trust are reshaping the sector – and the choices universities and government need to make now to secure a sustainable future. Register here.

This blog was kindly authored by Professor Faten Ghosn and Professor Silke Paulmann, both of the University of Essex.

Economic growth has once again become Britain’s defining policy challenge. In his first speech as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham pledged to build ‘a new economic model’ through re-industrialising Britain, devolving power and reforming education to help more young people into work. That agenda inevitably raises questions about the skills needed to drive future prosperity and, crucially, whether the economy is creating opportunities that make full use of those skills.

Against this backdrop, in June, the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ (IFS) published its report on the lifetime returns to undergraduate degrees. Predictably, much of the debate has focused on whether university is still worth it. Yet by concentrating almost exclusively on the return to a degree, we risk missing a much bigger issue: whether Britain is creating an economy capable of making full use of the graduates its universities produce.

The IFS report does not reveal a single return to higher education. Returns vary considerably between subjects, institutions and individuals. Some graduates enjoy substantial lifetime earnings gains, while around one in four may not recover the financial costs of attending university. Those differences matter. But they also point to a deeper truth: the value of higher education cannot be understood by looking at universities alone.

The report measures the private financial returns to undergraduate study. That is an important measure of value, particularly for prospective students and policymakers. But it is not the whole story. Higher education delivers benefits that extend well beyond income. A landmark review published in The Lancet Public Health found that every additional year of education reduces adult mortality risk by almost 2 per cent, while UK research shows graduates are more likely to adopt healthier lifestyles and age more successfully. They are not simply private gains. Healthier populations reduce pressure on the NHS, remain economically active for longer, and participate more actively in civic life. The returns to higher education therefore extend beyond graduate salaries to the health, resilience and productivity of the wider economy.

Britain’s debate about universities has become strangely one-sided. We scrutinise the supply of graduate skills – what universities teach, whether degrees pay, whether graduates are ‘work-ready’. Far less attention is paid to the demand side: whether Britain’s economy is creating enough high-skilled opportunities to make full use of the talent universities produce.

Graduate outcomes are co-produced. Universities develop knowledge, skills and capability; employers create jobs that utilise those capabilities; government shapes the conditions through industrial strategy, innovation policy, regional investment and support for business growth. The returns to higher education emerge from the interaction between all three.

Seen in this light, the IFS findings take on a different meaning. If some graduates struggle to realise strong economic returns, this may tell us something not only about the courses they studied, but also about the economy into which they graduated. Graduate salaries reflect labour market demand, regional economic performance, business investment and productivity growth. A degree cannot realise its full value if the economy fails to create opportunities that require graduate-level skills.

Yet, public debate often assumes precisely the opposite. Universities are routinely expected to justify themselves through the earnings of their graduates in a way that few other public institutions are. We do not judge hospitals solely by the future tax revenues of the patients they treat, nor transport infrastructure only by the salaries of those who use it. We recognise that these institutions create capabilities and opportunities whose benefits ripple through society and the economy. Universities should be understood in much the same way.

None of this absolves universities of responsibility. Students deserve clear information about employment prospects, and universities must continue improving teaching, embracing new technologies responsibly, strengthening links with employers and ensuring graduates leave with skills relevant to an AI-driven economy.

But employability is only half of the equation. The other half lies beyond the university campus. It depends on whether Britain is building an economy capable of absorbing and rewarding graduate talent through investment in innovation, research and development, technology adoption, entrepreneurship and regional economic growth. In a recent article, John Burn-Murdoch, highlighted that graduate wage premiums have remained resilient across countries including Canada, France, the Netherlands, Spain and the United States even as participation in higher education has expanded. Britain stands out not because its universities have become less effective, but because productivity growth has stalled and high-value job creation has lagged behind comparable economies.

title: ‘The show choir definitely helped me’: the dos and don’ts of joining student societies
summary:
Signing up for university clubs and societies is a surefire way to meet like-minded people, boosting your social life and your CV at a stroke

Clubs and societies are a huge part of student life, though many miss out on them. According to a recent survey by Savanta, 67% of students, particularly those who live at home while studying at university, did not take part in societies, clubs or social activities at least once during term.

But if you ask the students and graduates who did benefit from extracurricular activities, they’ll tell you they are well worth the trip. Here are their dos and don’ts.

full_text:
Clubs and societies are a huge part of student life, though many miss out on them. According to a recent survey by Savanta, 67% of students, particularly those who live at home while studying at university, did not take part in societies, clubs or social activities at least once during term.

But if you ask the students and graduates who did benefit from extracurricular activities, they’ll tell you they are well worth the trip. Here are their dos and don’ts.

What to do

Sign up to more than just one. “You’ll probably end up joining more societies than you might be able to keep up throughout your time at university and that’s totally normal,” says Dell*, 25, a graduate of Japanese from Oxford University. “I definitely recommend joining at least two, because it is such a great way to meet people. It can be quite a great escape from when you’re feeling stressed about university work or other situations.”

Izzy Clark, 20, an anthropology student at the University of Aberdeen, agrees. “Join maybe three or four and then decide whether or not you like them, because it’s harder to join the societies midway through the semester after they’ve settled into a routine,” she says. “I had no idea whether or not I would enjoy joining the show choir, as I wasn’t a particularly confident person, but I found that it definitely helped me.”

Remember, everyone is in the same boat, says Isabella*, 26, a film-making graduate from the University of Sussex. “I think just realising that can help when you’re going around the freshers’ fair,” she says. “The people running the socs want people to join, so I think it’s good to just go up to their desk and say you’ll join.”

Put societies on your CV. Even activities that aren’t directly related to your chosen field can end up making the difference in a future job search, says Alex Frost, 24, a history graduate from the University of Edinburgh. Frost says his experience on the committee of his orchestra was more useful in his current career working at a prison than anything he learned on his degree course. He learned “a lot of skills in how to interact with people and leading projects,” he says. “For example we had someone who needed financial support to buy an instrument and we dealt with that. We also organised a tour to the Lake District. And that’s the sort of stuff that you have to do in a real job. You have to get out of your comfort zone.”

Isabella’s time as social secretary of her cheerleading squad gave her leadership and organisation skills, she adds. “I became social sec around the time when people realised you could make a career out of social media – and it was really helpful for me to put on my CV.”

Ask for taster sessions first to cut costs. Radhika*, 22, a medicine student at Queen’s University Belfast, advises freshers to first ask for taster sessions before joining any clubs. “Asking if they’ve got any free taster events allows you to see if you’d like to join that one and potentially commit to membership. It just means you’re saving money, especially considering how expensive everything is nowadays.”

And try meeting other members online first, says Martha Page, 23, who graduated from the Lancaster University: “My main advice is to join WhatsApp group chats and connect with people online first.” Page, who is blind and suffers from anxiety, says this helped “take the pressure out” for her when joining a new group felt daunting. “Before the session, that can open some doors so I would advise anyone to do that first.”

What not to do

Don’t ignore sport just because you’re not an athlete, Isabella advises. “As a thoroughly unsporty 18-year-old, I somehow settled on one of the two cheerleading groups at my university,” she says. “I was as coordinated as a newborn foal. We were not a competitive cheer club, and we didn’t have a coach, but we had big sparkly bows and each other.”

Don’t feel like you have to drink the whole time. “I definitely think a lot of student culture revolves around drinking,” says Dell, looking back on her slightly underwhelming time at a Marxist society. “Regardless of whether it’s a structured society or not. But I think the less structured societies are more susceptible to just becoming excuses to get really drunk together.”

But whatever you do, don’t go without trying any societies at all. As Isabella says: “My only bad experience is I wish I had done even more.”

*Surnames withheld on request

title: UK government to offer clearer guidance on student loans after repayment row
summary:
Criticism of three-year threshold repayment freeze in England prompts update to guidance warning terms and conditions could change

University students taking out student loans in England are to be warned that the terms and conditions could change so they are better informed about what they are signing up to, the government has said.

In July, a report by MPs said slideshows that compared student loan repayments to the cost of a mobile phone contract, and YouTube videos that did not mention the fact that conditions could be altered amounted to mis-selling by the government.

Continue reading...
full_text:
University students taking out student loans in England are to be warned that the terms and conditions could change so they are better informed about what they are signing up to, the government has said.

In July, a report by MPs said slideshows that compared student loan repayments to the cost of a mobile phone contract, and YouTube videos that did not mention the fact that conditions could be altered amounted to mis-selling by the government.

The Treasury committee’s investigation followed a furore last November when the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, announced that the repayment threshold on plan 2 loans in England would be frozen at the current threshold, £29,385 for three years from April 2027.

Some students had been led to believe that the thresholds would rise in line with inflation each year.

The committee’s report said the government had a “moral obligation” to reverse the freeze to maintain students’ trust and honour the terms under which the loans were sold to them.

In its response, published on Sunday, the government acknowledged the difficulties faced by graduates repaying loans, and said it kept “all aspects of the student finance system under review”, but did not commit to any change in policy.

It said it would redesign the guidance for new students to make it clear and unambiguous.

However it rejected the committee’s recommendation to issue new loans on a contractual basis so that terms could not be changed at a later date, saying it needed to be able to adapt the system to changing economic circumstances in order to keep taxpayers’ contributions stable.

In August, 121 MPs and peers from across party lines signed a letter to the new chancellor, John Healey, calling on him to urgently review the repayment system.

The letter said the frozen thresholds combined with inflation-linked interest rates meant young teachers, nurses, engineers, and entrepreneurs were facing “historically high” effective marginal tax rates.

“For many middle-income graduates, the combination of income tax, national insurance, and student loan repayments means they see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise,” it said.

Responding to the government’s commitment to offer clearer guidance, the chair of the Treasury committee, Meg Hillier, said: “The commitment to right a historical wrong by updating the information so that prospective students are properly informed before taking out a massive loan is an important step forward.

“Unfortunately, though, it doesn’t help graduates who are angry that they didn’t receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing.”

Hillier welcomed the fact that a reversal of the threshold freeze had not been ruled out.

“I recognise that finances are tight but I continue to urge the chancellor to look at this again. I sincerely hope he will use his upcoming budget to give graduates some much-needed breathing space.”

A government spokesperson said: “We are taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university, starting with improved and clearer guidance for those taking out loans.

“That includes increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants to expand opportunities for people from all backgrounds, and [we have] raised the repayment threshold for plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021.

“We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way.”

title: OPINION: We’ve been treating college as a career plan, but it’s failing too many students
summary:
In one of Denver’s wealthiest suburbs, where median family income tops $150,000 and nearly every kid is expected to go to college, students are now lining up for trade certifications. Their parents aren’t worried; in fact, most of them are championing the move. For decades, Americans have been treating college as a career plan, spurred […]

The post OPINION: We’ve been treating college as a career plan, but it’s failing too many students appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
In one of Denver’s wealthiest suburbs, where median family income tops $150,000 and nearly every kid is expected to go to college, students are now lining up for trade certifications.

Their parents aren’t worried; in fact, most of them are championing the move.

For decades, Americans have been treating college as a career plan, spurred by the “college for all” movement — a decades-long educational and political push that aimed to make a four-year college degree the standard expectation and primary goal for all high school students. The data show that it doesn’t work.

Although 88 percent of college freshmen say getting a good job is “a main reason” they enrolled, more than half of college graduates are underemployed a year out, working jobs that don’t require a degree. A decade later, 45 percent still are.

These aren’t students who dropped out or gave up. They did everything right and still couldn’t find their footing.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

The problem isn’t that college doesn’t matter. It’s that college has become an expensive career exploration strategy, with no exit ramp for students who may need one. No wonder confidence in higher education is slipping.

It does not have to be that way. The opportunities for those without a four-year degree are exploding. The U.S. faces an annual shortage of nearly 712,000 workers with certificates and associate degrees in fields where workers without a bachelor’s degree can earn upward of $55,000 a year, Georgetown University’s Center on Education and the Workforce found.

The jobs are there. The pathways to them are not.

One course correction to the “college for all” movement is playing out in Denver’s Cherry Creek neighborhood, where high school students are participating in a program that offers real-world skill building and trade certifications, ranging from computer science to aviation to health science.

Students split their time between the program and their regular classes, with transportation provided to and from their home high school. When I visited the program, I met three students who were all headed down different paths: One intended to pursue a bachelor’s degree for engineering. Another was interested in an associate degree for construction management. The third was excited to earn an industry credential to become a chef.

The common thread they shared was that they were all locked in on their career paths. They had real experience in the field from the Cherry Creek Innovation Campus and clarity that they were moving in the right direction. Most Cherry Creek students still end up enrolling in college, but they do so with direction and purpose.

Georgetown’s ROI data shows that associate degrees and certificates often deliver a higher return on investment than bachelor’s degrees in the first 10 years after completion, although the data also shows that ROI for bachelor’s degrees pulls ahead at 15 years and then widens the gap thereafter.

That nuance matters: For students who need economic traction now, shorter-term credentials can be the smarter first move.

The “college for all” movement, while well-intentioned, has created a false binary between academic preparedness and workforce skills. Programs like Cherry Creek’s not only improve engagement in high school and college-going rates but also offer a more defined pathway into the workforce.

In my former role as CEO of a public charter school foundation, I was fortunate to be able to support the journeys of hundreds of students from college acceptance to college graduation. But it’s the journeys that didn’t work out as planned that have stuck with me the most.

Take, for example, the experience of a student from Oakland who I met through our career coaching program. She grew up wanting to be a nurse and had enrolled in a nursing program for a bachelor of science degree, diligently setting out on her long-awaited career path and becoming the first in her family to go to college.

But she had never been exposed to real-world healthcare or nursing work in high school, and she got two years into her program before realizing nursing wasn’t for her. She transferred to a community college, worked at a fast-food restaurant, and went through what she now calls “a lost phase.”

Two years gone; not because she failed, but because the system never gave her a chance to figure out her path before she enrolled. What’s worse, most students in this situation are left saddled with student loan debt. We can do better.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is projected

If we want to meet the needs of a rapidly shifting economy — one in which college graduates can’t find good-paying jobs and employers can’t find graduates with the right skill set — we need to stop treating college and career readiness as separate tracks.

It’s time for families to stop picturing shop class when they hear “vocational training.” That’s a stigma born from a past of underfunded, poorly constructed programs that filtered kids out of opportunities rather than into them.

Today those programs look vastly different. Take, for example, nonprofit Ridgeline’s maritime career exploration program for high school students in the San Francisco Bay Area, where rising 11th and 12th graders get hands-on paid career experience in a variety of maritime fields such as ship engineering, ferry and container ship operations and port management. Some maritime jobs require apprenticeships; others require a degree from nearby Cal Poly Maritime Academy. Many pay six figures.

It’s time to set a new standard: Every high school should offer students the opportunity to graduate with a diploma and an industry-recognized credential or documented work experience.

Honor the choice to skip college while giving those who want a degree more purpose. Everyone wins.

Patrick O’Donnell is CEO and co-founder of Ridgeline, a nonprofit that connects Bay Area students from underserved communities to high-wage, high-demand careers.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

This story about college and careers was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for Hechinger’s weekly newsletter.

title: Rise in abuse of election candidates is ‘changing politics’ in England
summary:
Electoral Commission finds abuse, particularly of women, minority ethnic and disabled people, is affecting candidates’ behaviour

Abuse and intimidation of election candidates is “a serious and growing concern”, the Electoral Commission has said, as a review of this year’s local and mayoral elections in England revealed a surge in threats to those who stood.

More than half of the candidates for Labour or Reform UK reported abuse while those most likely to be targeted were women, people from minority ethnic backgrounds and those with disabilities.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Abuse and intimidation of election candidates is “a serious and growing concern”, the Electoral Commission has said, as a review of this year’s local and mayoral elections in England revealed a surge in threats to those who stood.

More than half of the candidates for Labour or Reform UK reported abuse while those most likely to be targeted were women, people from minority ethnic backgrounds and those with disabilities.

A report by the commission said candidates described being spat at and verbally and physically assaulted. It found that levels of abuse had reached the point where it was changing the behaviour of people standing in elections.

“I had to take my husband out on the door this time, which was a first,” said one candidate, who was among a third of those who said they may not stand for election again because of harassment or intimidation.

They added: “I felt quite independent previously, but there was so much anger from men of an older age at the door and some younger men, all disillusioned by politics and let down.

“I did understand that, but it was the anger and insults and close confrontation at times which was so aggressive. I feel I have to protect myself in public and not be on my own, for the first time in local politics, and will never put myself in any vulnerable places on my own again.”

Female candidates were more likely to change their behaviour over such concerns. More than three-quarters (79%) said they avoided campaigning on their own at least once, compared with 46% of male candidates, while 57% avoided speaking on controversial topics, compared with 32% of men.

Vijay Rangarajan, the chief executive of the Electoral Commission, said: “Our single biggest worry now is this rise in abuse and intimidation. It’s not directed at any one party and there seems to be a variety of causes.”

He said there was an increasing trend towards the “othering” of political opponents, “literally, a dehumanisation” and a blurring of the boundaries of civility, in some cases driven by social media.

“I think we’re going to see a kind of complete blurring of the online and offline worlds,” he said. “We’ve seen people in the real world walk down the street filming someone to produce an online video. And then when others see that online video, they get very angry and they go and start following someone else down the streets. So this kind of real, complete interaction between online and offline is a real feature.”

Rangarajan said he was struck by two particular cases. One was a disabled candidate who said they were threatened on the doorstep but “couldn’t run away” because of their disability. Another was a candidate who was targeted on social media and whose daughter called from school to say she had seen the online abuse and people were calling her parent a racist, fascist and Nazi.

The commission made a number of recommendations, including calling on social media companies to do more to tackle the online abuse of candidates by developing rapid response protocols, and calling on parties to urge their members to respect other campaigners.

The review found 59% of Reform UK and 54% of Labour candidates told of personally experiencing inappropriate behaviour, harassment or threats to their security, followed by 42% of Greens, 37% of independents, 26% of Tories and 22% of Liberal Democrats.

Rangarajan said the changes made by some candidates in how they campaigned was affecting local politics.

“It takes away, in some cases, things like meeting your candidate, which is really important in our politics. The second thing is it definitely affects women much more and ethnic minority candidates too, and even more if you’re both. People are stopping wanting to be candidates because of this and that’s a real problem,” he said.

Rangarajan called for a “multi-partisan approach” from parties.

“We’re all up for really robust debate, that’s what the whole election is about and it wouldn’t work if it wasn’t … but it’s got to have a modicum of respect to it as well and there are some things which are really unacceptable, like following someone’s family down the street, for example, trying to video them, or posting people death threats.”

On the upside, the report found that voters continue to be satisfied with how elections are run, with 94% of voters in England expressing satisfaction with the voting process, similar to 2025 (95%) and the last comparable elections in 2022 (96%).

Nevertheless, voters remain concerned about the accuracy of election information. More than half of those surveyed said they had seen misinformation, and one in 10 said they had seen deepfake material.

title: Readers reply: what have been the most prescient or accurate predictions of the future?
summary:
The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the art of soothsaying, prognostication and futurism

This week’s question: What would be the most useful superpower?

‘Fingertip shopping will be one of the many homemakers’ conveniences. This video console will be channelled into the store of her choice …” I’ve always been fascinated by this 1967 video (not 1969, as the label says) which accurately foresaw the advent of online shopping, CCTV, fax/email and electronic banking. (It was a little less prescient in its assumption of gender roles – wife shops, husband pays – but we’ll let that slide.) The video, entitled 1999AD, was made by the Philco-Ford company, an American electronics firm that started off in radios and moved into appliances and TVs. I’ve often wished the writer of this short film could see the world as it is in 2026. What are some other predictions that have come spookily close to the truth? Ann, Devon

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

Continue reading...
full_text:
‘Fingertip shopping will be one of the many homemakers’ conveniences. This video console will be channelled into the store of her choice …” I’ve always been fascinated by this 1967 video (not 1969, as the label says) which accurately foresaw the advent of online shopping, CCTV, fax/email and electronic banking. (It was a little less prescient in its assumption of gender roles – wife shops, husband pays – but we’ll let that slide.) The video, entitled 1999AD, was made by the Philco-Ford company, an American electronics firm that started off in radios and moved into appliances and TVs. I’ve often wished the writer of this short film could see the world as it is in 2026. What are some other predictions that have come spookily close to the truth? Ann, Devon

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

Readers reply

I have a copy of a primary school reading book from the early 1990s that not only predicted online shopping, but that we would also be emailing the local library for research on our homework. The library staff would even be able to fax a reply! AnneTifa

How about Prof James Ephraim Lovelock and his Gaia hypothesis? ANZAC69

Kingdom Come by JG Ballard without a doubt. Never read it? Have a look. bricklayersoption

It wasn’t exactly a prediction, but in Star Trek during my childhood they were using their handheld communicators for the “Beam me up, Scotty” message. These days, everyone has devices like Kirk’s and Spock’s. Nerdvanian

It was certainly prescient. Design team members at Apple have actually cited Star Trek’s communicator and Spock’s tricorder when talking about their desire to create a device like the iPhone and iPad. Adults realising their childhood fantasies … FrankieandDexy

When US shares were going crazy before the 1929 crash, a journalist asked Joseph Kennedy (JFK’s father): “What will happen to the stock market in the future?” Kennedy replied, “It will fluctuate.” Can’t say that he was wrong there. PeteTheBeat

My West Country father-in-law has a similar response to queries about the weather: “It’ll clear up and rain.” SpoilheapSurfer

George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four. LiveInWonder

Yes, in part, although I think there’s much more Huxley about in our time. Be quiet and take the “soma” (smartphones, social media), the shallow obsessions with appearance, shiny acquisitions and entertainment, etc. bricklayersoption

Reckon Aldous Huxley, with control through entertainment and hedonism as opposed to Orwell’s more directly oppressive alternative, turned out to be pretty close to the mark. SalfordGeoff

The NWRA (The North Will Rise Again) is a track on the album Grotesque (After the Gramme) released by the Fall in 1980. The lyrics by renegade genius Mark E Smith outline the events of a fictional violent uprising by the north of Britain against the south. Two of these events seemed spookily prescient on 15 June 1996. In the morning, an IRA bomb badly damaged the Arndale Centre in Manchester; in the afternoon, Scotland fans gathered in London’s Soho and Trafalgar Square after the match against England at Wembley in Euro 96, and skirmishes with England fans ensued. In the song, Smith had described both the razing of the Arndale Centre, and the streets of Soho which “reverberated with drunken Highland men” (he omitted to mention the drunken English men who also turned up). Matt, Amsterdam

While it was never intended to depict an imagined future more than a few years ahead of its time, Sinclair Lewis’s 1935 novel It Can’t Happen Here can’t fail but be read during Trump’s second presidency as a sustained act of clairvoyance – if inevitably uneven, it is on the whole remarkably on the money. It isn’t only that Buzz Windrip’s moral character and the strategies he and his supporters deploy in taking and attempting to consolidate power strike repeated resonances – although the parallels here are startling enough. It’s also his prescience (as signalled in the book’s title) about the extent of his more liberal-minded characters’ lack of prescience that makes Sinclair’s novel a truly spooky – as well as salutary – read. fainthope

The Simpsons predicting Trump’s presidency has to be right up there with the best. Thirdhandluke

Not really a prediction, but I used to have a long commute by train – about 100 minutes each way. I used to think that it would be great if you could watch last night’s TV while you travelled. It only took 20 years or so for that to be a reality. PeteTheBeat

Private James Frazer of Dad’s Army. We’re doomed. StanEthel

The exposing of Hitler and his socialist veil was enacted by many but, in particular, Otto Strasser. He predicted the rise of fascism, the banning of the left and much else that followed. slojdare

The return of Halley’s comet in 1758. English astronomer Edmond Halley used Newton’s laws of gravity and planetary motions to predict the return of a comet he had observed in 1682. It will return in 2061 on its regular 76-year journey around the sun. Sagarmatha1953

In 1912, the Russian futurist poet Velimir Khlebnikov published a short dialogue titled Teacher and Student: A Conversation. In it, he proposed a fantastic mathematical philosophy of history, one of whose rules was that states and empires collapse every 365 (+/-48) years. Hence, Khlebnikov asks in 1912, “In the year 554, the kingdom of the Vandals was subjugated. Should we not expect the fall of the state in 1917?”

A few years later, in 1915, Khlebnikov’s partner in Russian futurism, Vladimir Mayakovsky, published his long poem A Cloud in Trousers, one of whose stanzas goes as follows:

Where men’s sight falls short,

Wearing the revolutions’ thorny crown,

Leading at the head of the hungry horde,

The year 1916 is coming around.

Mayakovsky was one year off; Khlebnikov was spot-on. Roman Vater, Cambridgeshire

Simon and Garfunkel’s The Sound of Silence. I’m just waiting for the scribbles to appear on the London tube. Porthos

I think the writing team of Frederik Pohl and Cyril M Kornbluth had some outstanding ones (strangely, I’ve never liked the work of either author working alone so much). The Space Merchants, its sequel The Merchants’ War and the less well-known Gladiator-at-Law all score some really blistering satirical hits – or at least, they were meant to be satirical in an “If this goes on …” kind of way. However, I still think the crown has to go to EM Forster for The Machine Stops, bearing in mind that it was published in 1909 when most of us in the UK were still lighting our streets with gas. SpoilheapSurfer

Snow Crash by Neal Stephenson was a pretty accurate prediction of the evolution of the internet, particularly virtual worlds. It’s also a cracking read that stands up today. Stumpysheep

Amy Hunt predicting she would win four European Athletics golds: 100m, 200m, 4x100m mixed relay, 4x100m relay. Steve4000

Generally, only very near-term predictions (less than 50 years) are feasible – often compounded by things like the “Star Trek effect”, where things are less prediction and more inspiration for children to create within their own lifetime the fictional technology they saw. So truly deep historical predictions are incredibly rare, or only very general, and take some generous interpretation by the beholder.

The only exception I can think of is Svante August Arrhenius, who in 1896 observed: “If the quantity of carbonic acid increases in geometric progression, the augmentation of the temperature will increase nearly in arithmetic progression.” By using infrared observations of the moon, he then calculated how much of infrared is captured by CO2 and water (H2O) vapour in Earth’s atmosphere, leading him to be the first person to correctly conclude that human-caused CO2 emissions from burning fossil fuels are large enough to swamp the cooling by orbital variations that precipitate ice ages and so cause long-term global warming. Ironically, he was trying to prove the opposite – that CO2 could only explain the temperature rises of inter-glacial periods.

He further tried to inform the public in 1906 with his book Världarnas Utveckling (Worlds in the Making), describing his “hot-house” theory of the atmosphere, aimed at a popular audience.

Even though Arrhenius’s estimates were very broad and lacked the details of modern techniques, with their many competing heating and cooling drivers, broadly they cancel out and agree surprisingly well with his original estimate that increases of 2.5-3 times of CO2 will cause a temperature rise of 8–9C in the Arctic.

title: Cultivating Student Resilience: Practical Strategies for Well-Being
summary:
The introduction of self-regulation and stress-management strategies into higher education curricula has recently come into focus as a necessary component of promoting resilience and preventing future professional burnout (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021; Egan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025). In addition to enhancing academic performance, evidence-based regulation strategies could help mitigate the effects of […]

The post Cultivating Student Resilience: Practical Strategies for Well-Being appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The introduction of self-regulation and stress-management strategies into higher education curricula has recently come into focus as a necessary component of promoting resilience and preventing future professional burnout (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021; Egan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025). In addition to enhancing academic performance, evidence-based regulation strategies could help mitigate the effects of the high-stakes, high-stress environment inherent in college and post-graduate education (Chongjin et al., 2025), and learned self-regulation skills may carry over into the professional environment after graduation (Emerson et al., 2023). Integrating short, reflective activities and simple self-regulation practices into established curricula may be an effective strategy for providing students with helpful and actionable means to foster self-awareness and well-being (Egan et al., 2021; Gilani, 2025). This article aims to discuss how stress management can be a tool for building resilience and promoting deep learning, outline several practical approaches that educators can use to weave self-care into existing curricula, and introduce several strategies to foster students’ self-exploration and awareness.

Unmanaged and excessive stress impairs the cognitive flexibility needed for deep learning (Zhang et al., 2025).To mitigate these effects on students, resilience skills such as cognitive reframing and emotional regulation can be taught as effective techniques to support academic success (Egan et al., 2022).

Many of the self-reflection skills that help increase stress tolerance are closely linked to those of metacognition, a fundamental component of self-regulated learning (SRL). In a systematic review of interventions to improve SRL, 74% of the analyzed interventions focused on metacognitive skills as a means of supporting self-regulation in students (Simón-Grábalos et al., 2025). SRL boosts confidence, enhances critical thinking, and improves student performance. SRL also helps learners develop essential career skills such as solving complex problems and effective time management (Gagnon et al, 2026).

Teaching adult learners basic principles of brain function and neuroplasticity may help them reframe stress, regulate emotions, and improve self-efficacy and optimism for change (Tabibnia, 2024). Leveraging the brain’s ability to reorganize in response to practiced experiences can be framed for learners as a viable pathway to build resilience and manage stressors. This strategy reflects the concept of growth mindset-a belief that intelligence is both malleable and improvable (Ng, 2018). Thus, emphasizing and encouraging a growth mindset could be a powerful tool for helping learners navigate both academic and future professional challenges.

Demanding schedules and packed curricula make it difficult for students and educators to prioritize stress management and wellness practices, despite recognizing their inherent value (Chongjin et al., 2025). Transitioning from a theoretical understanding of the importance of self-care to the practical application of building student resilience, requires stress management to be viewed and treated as a professional competence rather than an individual responsibility (Jian et al., 2025). Intentionally integrating self-care concepts and methods into existing course curricula and resources is a key to normalizing the prioritization of mental, emotional, and physical health for students. The following actionable methods for embedding self-care initiatives into existing class time are simple and effective.

Syllabus Resourcing

Include a section on the front page of each course syllabus that acknowledges the demands of the course. Explicitly list campus mental health resources and encourage their use.

Embracing Error

Making mistakes is an important component of learning. Changing the wording when addressing errors is a simple way to create an inclusive learning environment and build critical thinking skills (Chong et al., 2025)

Be curious: “What makes you say that?” Encourages sharing and dialogue, allowing faculty to give feedback that focuses on critical thinking and processing skills, rather than the binary view of “right” and “wrong”.

Normalizing Uncertainty

Ambiguity is a hallmark of many professions, and building tolerance for it is a critical skill. Letting students know that knowing how to find a reliable answer to a question or solution to a problem is often more valuable and important than knowing the answer immediately (Ng, 2018). Incorporating case-based learning with multiple plausible approaches is an effective way to model this principle for students (Hsu & Goldsmith, 2021).

Model Vulnerability

Hearing faculty share their professional missteps or errors and how they were corrected or turned into learning moments is a powerful way to come alongside students and show that mistakes are not personal failings, and to model their effective use.

Physical Grounding Techniques

Lead short, evidence-based physical grounding techniques to help students decrease tension and stress (Bently et al., 2023).

Box breathing (American Heart Association, 2024).

Body scan (Masterclass, 2022).

Somatic self care (Johns Hopkins Medicine, n.d.).

Scan for Signals

Encourage students to take a moment prior to tests and quizzes to “scan” their emotional state and stress level help them become aware of and monitor their emotional and physical responses to stressful situations. Encourage them to use physical grounding techniques before, during, and after high-stakes testing.

Write it Down

Promote short reflective journaling assignments, giving prompts to help students identify what study techniques work for them, what areas of their training cause the most stress (Gilani, 2025; Sage & Sele, 2015), and help by suggesting possible solutions or avenues of exploration, including seeking higher levels of care with professional counseling.

Create Community

Provide short prompts for structured, time-limited peer conversations where students discuss both course topics and the emotional stressors of the week. (Chong et al, 2025; Gómez et al, 2024).

Cultivating resilience in students prepares them for lifelong learning and normalizes the practices of attending to personal wellness and maintaining mental health. By incorporating simple practices into classroom curricula and placing value on self-reflection, the role of making mistakes as part of a natural learning process, and showing students how stress can prevent deep learning, educators can provide life skills that could help prevent burnout in professional practice (Chong et al., 2025).

Additional Resource from the Author

Lee Lipton’s Mindfulness in Education Toolkit

Call to Action for Readers: Choose one of the above ideas and put it into practice in your classes next week.

Lee Lipton is a certified physician associate with extensive experience in urgent care, family medicine, and women’s health, and a clinical instructor for the University of the Pacific’s Physician Assistant program. As an international corporate health educator, she presents trainings on resilience, mindfulness, and preventive care. Her professional interests include health behavior change and the impact of mindfulness on disease outcomes and clinician burnout. Lipton holds a Master’s degree from UC Davis and is currently pursuing a doctorate at the University of the Pacific. A published author, her work appears in the Journal of the American Academy of Physician Assistants.

title: Productive Friction: What Universities Must Protect in the Age of AI
